title: Project Brief Template
body:
# Project Brief Template

Use this template to produce a validated editorial brief before any drafting begins. Every field is required unless marked optional. The brief is the contract between discovery and production — every downstream agent reads it to understand what they are building and for whom.

---

## Goal

State the single primary outcome this document must achieve. This is not a description of the document — it is the job the document does. Write it as an outcome: "Enable [audience] to [do/decide/understand] [thing]." Avoid vague goals like "inform the reader" — be specific about what the reader must be able to do or believe after reading.

Example: "Enable a non-technical product manager to evaluate whether their team should adopt machine learning-based recommendation systems, and understand the key implementation tradeoffs."

---

## Audience

Define the audience by their relationship to the content — not by demographics. State: (1) what they already know, (2) what they do not know, (3) what they care about, (4) what skepticism or resistance they bring. This field governs voice, assumed knowledge, and argument structure.

Example: "Software engineers with 3+ years experience. Familiar with REST APIs and basic data modeling. Not familiar with ML pipelines or recommendation algorithms. Care about implementation complexity and maintenance burden. Skeptical of ML hype."

---

## Domain

Select the active domain from the supported list: general, internal, technical, dnd, card-game. The domain determines which style pack is loaded, which canon records apply, and which QA rubric is used.

---

## Tone

Specify the register and voice. Reference the applicable style pack rather than describing tone freehand. If the style pack is not yet loaded, describe: formality level (formal/semi-formal/conversational), stance (authoritative/exploratory/instructional), and any specific prohibitions (no humor, no first person, etc.).

---

## Scope — In Scope

List everything this document will cover. Be specific. "The history of X" is not specific. "The period from X to Y, covering [event A] and [decision B]" is specific. This field exists to prevent scope creep during drafting.

---

## Scope — Out of Scope

List everything this document will NOT cover, especially items a reader might expect to be covered. Out-of-scope declarations prevent section-drafter from expanding into adjacent areas and prevent QA from flagging intentional omissions as gaps.

---

## Constraints

List hard constraints on the output: word count ceiling/floor, format restrictions, regulatory or legal constraints, organizational style mandates, accessibility requirements, deadline constraints, any topics that must not be mentioned.

---

## Deliverables

List the specific output artifacts: the document title, format (markdown/docx/pdf/latex), target word count, number of sections, any companion artifacts (glossary, appendix, diagram). Each deliverable must match the goal — if the goal requires a decision memo, the deliverable must be a decision memo, not an article.

---

## Success Criteria

State how you will know this document succeeded. Criteria must be testable, not aspirational. Bad: "the document should be engaging." Good: "a reader unfamiliar with ML can read the document and correctly answer the five comprehension questions in the eval set." Include QA thresholds: minimum acceptable scores on reader and skeptic perspectives.

---

## Known Inputs

List all source material already available: prior research reports, existing drafts, reference documents, canon records, examples to follow or avoid. If a source is unavailable, flag it here so the discovery agent can classify it as B4 (missing source material).
